chapter: Tatum, Wiggins and Los Angeles friends
title: Tuba with the Newton-Carter group in Europe, and rapport with Gerald Wiggins
summary: Callender describes a woodwind and tuba group at Bracknell and says playing with Wiggins needs no signals, like Ellington's band.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: We were playing Reel 2 back a minute ago, and at the point where I asked you on Reel 2 how you feel about the bass as opposed to the tuba, and you said you loved them equally, and when you listened to your response, you said off the tape that it depended on whom you were working with. I wanted to ask you now if you would amplify on that.

And I went on to say that it would depend... It always depends upon whom you're working with, I guess. Because last July, I took a trip to Europe with one of the wildest groups I've ever played with in my life, and I think I had more fun than I've ever had before playing the tuba with anybody. In this group, we had a bassoon, tuba, clarinet, flute, and oboe. I played the tuba, of course, and James Newton played the flute and did most of the writing. John Carter, clarinet; I forgot to mention that. Charles Owens played the oboe and English horn, and sometimes soprano saxophone. We played Bracknell's, about 40 kilometers south of London, and the reception was so marvelous there, I couldn't believe it. I actually broke down and cried.

So much for the tuba, I wanted to mention... You asked me a question about the tuba and the bass. And here lately, I have had and have the pleasure of working with Gerald Wiggins, and that's as much fun as I've had since working

with Tatum, who was also a pretty decent piano player. So lately, I've played the Money Tree with Gerald and Herb Jeffries, and then we played another one at the Holiday Inn up in Ventura, and also we played a couple of weddings here and there and a couple of parties -- and I've just been really enjoying myself more than I can explain, really. You see, when Gerald and I work together, Gerald just... He doesn't have to call the tunes. There's some kind of signals. I couldn't begin to explain them. But he just starts, and I just happen... We happen to feel alike, I guess. Because I hear what he's doing, and we don't need any verbal communication to play together -- which I find to be marvelous.

Because that's the way I thought Duke Ellington used to start his band off. He would strike a note and never say a word, then all of a sudden he would bring his hand down, and the band would shower, and it was always a mystery to me how they knew what was going on. But now I think I understand, after having worked with Gerald. When you work with anybody for a long period of time, and you get so used to what's going on until certain sounds suggest certain things.
